I don't believe that the reason for the 3/5ths clause is pertinent to the topic at hand. I believe that the mere fact that it exists is pertinent to the topic at hand.

And I would add that, though not specifically stated in the Constitution, the principle that blacks were not fully-fledged people (which principle was actually the point of my post, with the Constitution only a notable, and probably ill-advised, example of it in action) was self-evidently central to the foundation of the nation as evidenced by the simple fact that the Constitutional rights granted to all people by the Bill of Rights were simply denied blacks.

If the Constitution had defined blacks as 3/5s of a person or otherwise codified slavery...

But the Constitution does not define any persons as any things or codify any things. (Nor, as you said in the last, does it in any way address the rights of the people - that's the Bill of Rights, which are amendments to the Constitution, and not the main body itself).

The Constitution defines the branches of the federal government and the offices that are to compose those branches, specifies the qualifications for those offices and the manner in which the officeholders are to be chosen, and lists the specific powers that are to be granted to those officeholders. The original intent was to limit the potential for abuse by clearly delineating the powers of the government. Since some (rightly) believed that that wasn't sufficient and that officeholders would claim powers not granted, the Bill of Rights was added to specify things that they could not limit, even if they did pretend to possess the power to limit them. And in order to drive that point home, the 10th amendment made it explicit that the powers not specifically granted to the federal government by the Constitution were to devolve to the states or the people. Fat lot of good that did, but still...

To the topic: the Constitution could not "define blacks as 3/5s of a person" broadly, because the Constitution does not define "persons" broadly at all. It only addresses the topic in one context - that of apportionment - and in that context it does make a distinction. That is the one and only context in which it does define a "person," so that is the one and only one that is pertinent to the topic at hand. That's why (in that context at least) I stand by my initial assertion.

Now - all that said (and I could go on much more about the Constitution - the common misconceptions of it are among my pet peeves), I will say that pointing to the Constitution as evidence was a poor move and is rightly contradicted, but not, I believe, on the grounds you've presented. The problem, as I've come to see it, is that the 3/5ths clause is not explicitly racist. It's obviously intended to deal with slaves, who were primarily (though not exclusively) black, but the distinction is not made on race, but on "free" status or the lack thereof. So it's weakly arguably racist by implication, but it's simply not explicitly so.

And all that said, my central point was merely that the statement that the nation was founded on racist principles is an accurate one - at least enough so that those who seek to challenge Sanders' rhetoric are not well-served by pretending that it's not. They'd be better served by pointing out that those principles were explicitly and deliberately overturned a century and a half ago, so it's arguably no more relevant that they existed at the time of the founding than it is that the founders wore powdered wigs and wrote with quills dipped in ink.

You specify exactly where we appear to diverge on this right in the beginning: "America's principles are, I would say, equivalent to its ideals..."

I wouldn't say that. I would say that its principles, at any given time, are the underlying and often more simply accepted than explicitly stated concepts from which its laws are built.

For instance, a principle of modern America is that the purported well-being of children possesses additional merit over the well-being of adults - that a thing that can be said to notably pose a nominal threat to children is, simply by that fact, of greater significance, and carries greater need, and justification, to be dealt with by the legal system.

I'm not sure that that's laid out explicitly anywhere, and I doubt that it is (other than in the common cliche, "But think of the children!). Rather, it's a principle underlying current US legal policy - a principle upon which legal decisions are often made.

That there were legal distinctions to be made between blacks and whites was obviously a principle that was in place at the founding of the nation, and in fact, it's obvious that that principle was held by the founders and the earliest governments, demonstrated, as I noted earlier, by the fact that the rights outlined in the Bill of Rights were quite simply generally not extended to blacks. And in fact, I would go so far as to argue that it's made even more clear that that was a fundamental principle of government at the time by the fact that it was not widely stated - laws apparently did not explicitly state that blacks were to be treated differently, yet they indisputably were, which means that it was such a widely held principle that it didn't even need to be explicitly stated in order to be understood. Rights and privileges that were granted to "the people" were withheld from blacks, and often without explicit command that they be withheld from blacks, so it was obviously simply assumed that that was the case, which can only be because that was an underlying principle of the legal system of the time.

The place where it gets questionable is the existence of free blacks. For the most part (and for all I know, to the full extent of the law) free blacks possessed all of the same legal rights as whites. It's certain that the distinction was really made based on free vs. slave status rather than on race, and that would seem to, and probably to some degree does, undermine the idea that the principles governing the extension of rights to individuals were fundamentally racist. However, even with that, I would argue that they continued to be fundamentally racist, simply because there existed the conception of "free" blacks, as an exceptional group, to be distinguished from the rest of the blacks. The need to make a distinction between a person who could prove himself to be "free" and a person who could not, and therefore was not, was itself certainly a racist distinction - one that black were subject to, while whites were not.

It strikes me there - a bit late in the exchange - that I should clarify my use of the term "racist." In a legal context, I use the term "racist" to describe any legal distinction that is made solely based on race - any exception to equal treatment under the law - no matter what it might be or in what "direction" it might lean - that is based on race. That might be part of the issue here too - there's often a sort of punitive sense to the word "racist" - that only that which is explicitly intended to bring harm, and often only if that harm is visited upon the nominally less powerful race by the nominally more powerful race, is to be considered "racist." I don't accept that. I believe, and use the word in this sense, that any distinction made based primarily on race is undeniably "racist."

So to sum up - I wouldn't argue that it's necessary that the legal documents of the time make explicit racist distinctions in order to demonstrate that racism was an accepted principle at the time. I would argue that it's only necessary that the legal system make those distinctions, and it's self-evident that it did indeed make those distinctions. Therefore, regardless of how explicit it might or might not have been in the phrasing of the laws, the mere existence of obvious legal distinctions based upon race demonstrates that unequal treatment based on race was a fundamental principle of the time, just as unequal treatment based on age (at least child vs. adult) is a fundamental principle of ours.

I got really interested in this problem a while ago. I wanted a smartphone that wouldn't spy on me.

It is technically feastible to wire the GPIO outputs on a Raspberry Pi to a Toby line Ublox 4g/GSM chip. Add a battery and screen and you have all the hardware for a smartphone.

The software would be archlinux for ARM7, but actually communicating with the chip would require writing about 1000 labor hours of code. You'd have to build up from step functions all the way to @ commands, then write a 4g network driver and GSM driver. Finally you would need to write texting and calling applications.

Understandably I dropped the idea when I finished the first draft of the software block diagram.
